examples.knowledge_point: Evaluating Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y Along Cartesian Curves
examples.problem:
If the path $C$ is a part of the parabola $y=x^2$ traversed from the point $A(0,0)$ to the point $B(1,1),$ evaluate the line integral 

$$
\displaystyle \int\limits_C (x+y)\,\mathrm{d}x + (x-y)\,\mathrm{d}y.
$$
examples.worked_solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y = x^2.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=t\,i+{t}^{2}\,j,\,t\in [0,1]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x+y)\,dx+(x-y)\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x+y)\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+(x-y)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}((x+y)\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+(x-y)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(t+{t}^{2})\cdot 1+(t-{t}^{2})\cdot 2t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}t+3{t}^{2}-2{t}^{3}\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+{t}^{3}-\frac{{t}^{4}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[\frac{1}{2}+1-\frac{1}{2}]-[0] \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem: If the path $C$ is the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}$ traversed from the point $A(0,0)$ to the point $B(4,2),$ then ${\int }_{C}{e}^{x+y}\,dx-{e}^{x+y}\,dy=$
feedback.worked_solution:
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=0\,i+0\,j$ and $b=4\,i+2\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =0\,i+0\,j+t(4\,i+2\,j-(0\,i+0\,j)) \\  & =4t\,i+2t\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x(t)=4t$ and $y(t)=2t$ along the segment.

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=4\,i+2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{e}^{x+y}\,dx-{e}^{x+y}\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{x+y}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t-{e}^{x+y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{x+y}(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{4t+2t}(4-2)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{6t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{{e}^{6t}}{3}\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{6(1)}}{3}-\frac{{e}^{6(0)}}{3} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{6}}{3}-\frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{6}-1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$
